case_study_insert.main_stem: Preston Gearbox Assemblies (PGB) is a worker cooperative in the automotive components sector, assembling gearboxes for commercial vehicles and supplying two domestic fleet operators, with a workforce of 42. Founded in 2011 by Isabel Preston, it operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. PGB plans to invest $540,000 in a robotic gear-assembly cell, financed by a $340,000 five-year bank loan and $200,000 of leasing. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $11.00 a unit and a selling price of $20.00, and produces 36,000 units a year. PGB faces absenteeism of 8% and a 2.7% defect rate in final gear assembly, which is straining its delivery schedule.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Assembly and HR Log — January 2025: 7,200 gear units were assembled with a defect rate of 2.7%; absenteeism reached 8% and staff turnover 11%. There were 19 formal quality complaints from commercial-vehicle customers. Average assembly time is 42 minutes per unit. A survey of 240 drivers and fleet buyers found 72% rate gear reliability as the top purchase factor and 55% would pay $0.70 more for a two-year warranty.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Preston Gearbox Assemblies as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank lifted the base rate from 3.75% to 4.50%, increasing loan and leasing costs. (2) The minimum wage rose 7.1% to $13.45 per hour. (3) Steel and aluminium input costs climbed 8.3% year-on-year, while road-freight costs rose 5.2% and commercial-vehicle production grew 1.8%.

questions.question_text: PGB plans to finance part of its robotic assembly cell with a bank loan. Explain two advantages for PGB of using leasing instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Leasing the $200,000 of equipment spreads payment over the asset's life and avoids a large immediate cash outflow, which matters when PGB's fixed costs are $240,000 a year and absenteeism is 8%. Cash is preserved for the 42-worker cooperative to tackle the 2.7% defect rate while the $340,000 loan is serviced.

Point 2: With leasing, the lessor normally maintains the robotic cell, shifting technical risk away from a small cooperative with no specialist engineering team. Isabel Preston can therefore adopt the $540,000 investment without tying up the cooperative's reserves, though the asset is not owned at the end and total payments may exceed a loan.

Leasing also suits a cooperative with 42 members because it avoids asking members for more capital while 19 complaints and 8% absenteeism must be solved. The $340,000 loan and fixed costs of $240,000 already require 26,666.67 units to break even, so preserving cash matters more than owning the asset at the end of the term.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: PGB is launching a two-year warranty on its gearboxes. Consider local newspaper advertising, a commercial-vehicle trade show, or fleet-operator direct mail. Which should PGB choose to promote the warranty? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local newspaper advertising: Cheap and accessible to the local community that includes many of the 42 workers' customers, but it reaches few fleet decision-makers and cannot explain the 72% reliability concern, so response would be weak.

Commercial-vehicle trade show: A stand lets PGB demonstrate gearboxes and the $0.70 warranty premium to the buyers behind the 19 complaints, building trust in person. Costs are high for a cooperative funding a $540,000 cell, and only a handful of the 240 surveyed buyers would attend.

Fleet-operator direct mail: Sending warranty details to the two domestic fleet operators and similar buyers targets exactly the 72% who rank reliability first and the 55% who would pay $0.70 more. It is low cost and measurable, though it depends on an up-to-date mailing list and gives no live demonstration.

With a 9,333-unit margin of safety, PGB cannot afford a campaign that fails to convert: each unit contributes $9.00, so a handful of extra fleet orders matters more than broad awareness. Direct mail reaches the buyers behind the 19 complaints and the 72% reliability ranking, and it can quote the $0.70 warranty precisely; neither a newspaper nor a show stand can be tied to the two domestic operators that drive sales.

Recommendation: PGB should choose direct mail to fleet operators, supported by a small trade-show presence. It reaches the specific buyers who value reliability at low cost. Newspaper advertising is rejected as untargeted; a full trade-show campaign is rejected as too expensive and they already have direct relationships with their fleet customers.

mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of at least two promotional routes applied to PGB with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Discussion of all three routes in context with a justified recommendation rejecting newspapers and the large trade-show spend.

questions.question_text: PGB has absenteeism of 8% and a flat structure with democratic leadership. Explain two benefits for PGB of using team working to improve motivation among its workforce of 42.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Team working lets the 42 members rotate gear-assembly tasks, reducing repetitive work and the 8% absenteeism that is straining the delivery schedule. Under Herzberg's motivators, greater variety and responsibility raise job satisfaction, which supports the democratic structure and helps hold the 2.7% defect rate while the $540,000 robotic cell is installed.

Point 2: Teams can discuss the 19 quality complaints and propose fixes, using the knowledge of operators who assemble 7,200 units a month. Shared ownership suits a worker cooperative and strengthens commitment, so the $9.00 contribution on each of 36,000 units is protected and the $0.70 warranty can be offered with confidence.

At 36,000 units divided by 42 workers, or 857.14 units per worker, even a small fall in absence protects output and the $9.00 contribution. Team working suits the flat democratic structure and helps meet the 55% of 240 surveyed buyers who would pay $0.70 more for a warranty, while the 19 complaints give a measurable target.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: PGB must cut its 8% absenteeism before the robotic cell arrives. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job college courses for its assemblers. Which should PGB choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the assembly bench teaches the exact gear-fitting routines the 42 workers need for the $540,000 robotic cell and keeps them productive, protecting output of 36,000 units and the 2.7% defect rate. It is cheap, but trainers are themselves assemblers, so their output falls and bad habits can be copied.

Off-the-job college courses: Structured courses give recognised certificates and up-to-date robotics knowledge, which could reduce the 8% absenteeism by raising morale and career prospects. The cost and loss of workers from the line, however, would disrupt the 42-minute assembly cycle and the 19 complaints target.

Progress should be tracked on the 8% absence figure, the 2.7% defect rate and the 7,200 units assembled, with refresher coaching if the 19 complaints do not fall. The insert provides no college fees or hours per course, so no total cost is asserted; the decision rests on keeping all 42 members productive while the $540,000 cell is installed. On-the-job coaching can be given shift by shift under democratic leadership, whereas sending assemblers away would break the 42-minute cycle and risk the 9,333-unit margin of safety while $240,000 of fixed costs must be covered.

A stable team of 42 also protects the $17.67 unit-cost benchmark.

Decision: PGB should choose on-the-job training first, with short college modules later for senior operators. It is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids removing staff while absenteeism is 8%; full off-the-job training is rejected because the lost assembly time and cost would undermine the $240,000 fixed-cost coverage and the 9,333-unit margin of safety.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies relevant factors with limited application to the named business.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of both training methods with application to PGB's absenteeism and output.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluation of both training options in context with a justified decision rejecting the alternative.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how PGB's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $240,000 ÷ ($20.00 − $11.00) = $240,000 ÷ $9.00 = 26,666.67 units. Answer: break-even output is 26,666.67 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $20.00 − $11.00 = $9.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $9.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways PGB's management can use this cost, break-even and productivity data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the break-even output of 26,666.67 units with actual production of 36,000 units, giving a margin of safety of 9,333.33 units, so they know how far demand can fall before PGB makes a loss.
2. Contribution per unit of $9.00 shows what each unit adds towards fixed costs of $240,000; for illustration, a $1.00 price cut would reduce contribution to $8.00 and raise break-even to 30,000 units, letting managers test pricing before committing.
3. Average total cost of $17.67 a unit ($240,000 ÷ 36,000 units plus $11.00 variable cost) provides a benchmark each quarter to track the 8% absenteeism and 2.7% defect rate and decide whether rework is pushing unit cost above plan.
4. Labour productivity of 857.14 units per worker (36,000 units ÷ workforce of 42) shows whether the $540,000 investment can be handled by the existing team, or whether recruitment is needed before the wage bill rises.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 26,666.67 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $9.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 36,000 units; illustrative pricing and the $240,000 fixed costs; the $540,000 investment decision; and unit-cost and productivity benchmarking to tackle the 8% absenteeism and 2.7% defect rate.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate PGB's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has PGB's financial position improved? Which of the two ratios is the stronger evidence? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.69 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.81 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.00 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $96,000 inventories + $84,000 trade receivables + $30,000 cash = $210,000; 2025 current assets = $90,000 + $112,000 + $18,000 = $220,000. For 2024, $210,000 ÷ $140,000 = 1.50, and ($210,000 − $96,000) ÷ $140,000 = 0.81. For 2025, $220,000 ÷ $130,000 = 1.69, and ($220,000 − $90,000) ÷ $130,000 = 1.00. All source figures are the $'000 values in Appendix 2.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened on both measures, so PGB's short-term financial position has improved. Trade receivables rose from $84,000 to $112,000 and cash fell from $30,000 to $18,000, so the improved liquidity depends on collecting from the fleet operators; current liabilities fell from $140,000 to $130,000, which helps the $340,000 loan and leasing payments.
The acid test ratio is the stronger evidence of real improvement because it rose from 0.81 to 1.00 without relying on inventories, which are the least liquid current asset.

The ratios are a single snapshot with no sector comparator, and the 1.69 current ratio masks a fall in cash to $18,000. The $112,000 of receivables must be collected before leasing payments and the $340,000 loan can be met comfortably.

Conclusion: PGB's financial position has improved: both liquidity measures are higher in 2025 and the gain survives the exclusion of inventories. PGB should chase the larger receivables before committing more of the $540,000 plan.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies relevant factors with limited application to the named business.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for both years with some contextual comment on the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years, detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities, an explicit answer on the stronger ratio, and a justified conclusion.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for PGB of using robotic gear assembly instead of manual assembly.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Robotic assembly reduces variation, directly attacking the 2.7% defect rate and the 19 complaints, so more of the 36,000 gearboxes meet the 72% reliability expectation and the $9.00 contribution survives fixed costs of $240,000.

Disadvantage: Robots raise fixed costs and need the 42-strong workforce to be retrained while absenteeism is 8%, risking disruption to the 42-minute assembly cycle. The insert does not break down the $11.00 variable cost, so with steel and aluminium up 8.3% PGB cannot tell how much of its cost is exposed, making the $540,000 commitment harder to judge.

Robotics raises fixed costs above $240,000 and needs 26,666.67 units to break even, so the $540,000 investment must improve the 2.7% defect rate to be worthwhile. The insert gives no cycle-time saving, so none is claimed; the judgement rests on quality and the 72% reliability preference among the 240 surveyed buyers. If reliability slips, the $0.70 warranty premium would be lost.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.50%, the 7.1% minimum wage increase to $13.45 and the 8.3% rise in steel and aluminium input costs will affect PGB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
PGB faces three external changes reported in Appendix 3.

Base interest rate 3.75% to 4.50%: If the $340,000 five-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds 0.0075 × $340,000 five-year bank loan = $2,550 a year (0.0075 × 340,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $240,000 and the $540,000 investment, and a fixed-rate loan would avoid it completely, though future borrowing would cost more and customers may cut spending.

Minimum wage up 7.1% to $13.45: With a workforce of 42, this raises the wage bill on every production hour and cannot be avoided. The insert states neither hours worked nor individual pay rates, so no defensible annual total can be invented; against the given productivity of 857.14 units per worker, the rise is absorbable only if output per worker holds, otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $9.00 contribution per unit is squeezed.

8.3% steel and aluminium input costs: The insert does not decompose the $11.00 variable cost per unit, so only a labelled upper-bound illustration is honest: if the entire $11.00 were exposed, the rise would add 0.083 × $11.00 = $0.913 a unit, or $32,868 a year at 36,000 units. Even this upper bound exceeds the $2,550 interest saving, so input prices matter most for the cooperative.

Conclusion: the 8.3% rise in steel and aluminium input costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds on every one of the 36,000 units, directly erodes the $9.00 contribution that justifies the $540,000 plan, and dwarfs the $2,550 interest effect; the wage rise is material but cannot be quantified from the insert. Isabel Preston should negotiate input prices and use the $0.70 warranty premium to protect the $9.00 contribution.
